title: Minimum Subarrays in a Valid Split
statement:
Cut the integer array `nums` into contiguous, non-empty pieces (subarrays) so that every element lands in exactly one piece. Such a split is **valid** when, in every piece, the greatest common divisor of the piece's first element and its last element is greater than `1`. A piece of a single element `x` has `x` as both its first and last element, so it qualifies exactly when `x > 1`.

Return the smallest number of pieces in a valid split of `nums`, or `-1` if no valid split exists.
notes:
## Intuition

Only the two ends of a piece matter; whatever sits in the middle is irrelevant. Trying every way to cut the array is exponential, but the best split of a prefix only depends on where its last piece starts. So let `dp[i]` be the fewest pieces in a valid split of the first `i` elements. A piece `nums[start..end]` can be appended to any valid split of the first `start` elements whenever `gcd(nums[start], nums[end]) > 1`.

## Approach

1. Fill `dp` with `Infinity` ("impossible") and set `dp[0] = 0`: the empty prefix needs no pieces.
2. For each `end`, try every `start <= end` as the first index of the last piece.
3. Skip a `start` whose prefix `dp[start]` cannot be split.
4. If `nums[start]` and `nums[end]` share a factor, update `dp[end + 1]` with `dp[start] + 1`.
5. Return `dp[n]`, or `-1` if it is still `Infinity`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [2, 6, 3, 4, 3]`.

- `end = 0`: `gcd(2, 2) = 2`, so `dp[1] = 1`.
- `end = 1`: `gcd(2, 6) = 2` gives `dp[2] = 1`.
- `end = 2`: `gcd(2, 3) = 1` fails, `gcd(6, 3) = 3` gives `dp[1] + 1 = 2`, so `dp[3] = 2`.
- `end = 3`: `gcd(2, 4) = 2` gives `dp[4] = 1`.
- `end = 4`: `start = 0` fails because `gcd(2, 3) = 1`, so one piece is impossible. `start = 1` (`gcd(6, 3) = 3`) and `start = 2` (`gcd(3, 3) = 3`) both give `dp[5] = 1 + 1 = 2`.

So the answer is `dp[5] = 2`, for example the pieces `[2, 6]` and `[3, 4, 3]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n² · log V), where V is the largest value: every `(start, end)` pair runs one gcd.
- Space: O(n) for `dp`.

## Pitfalls

- A single element is a valid piece unless it is `1`; do not require pieces of length two or more.
- If `nums[0]` or the last element is `1`, no piece can start or end there, so the answer is `-1`.
- Greedily making the first piece as long as possible is wrong; the DP is needed to compare all choices.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `gcd` | Euclid's greatest common divisor |
| `n` | length of `nums` |
| `dp[i]` | fewest pieces for the first `i` elements (`Infinity` if impossible) |
| `end` | index of the last element of the current piece |
| `start` | index of the first element of the current piece |
